# ui::Window

Header: `winui/ui/Window.hpp`.

The logical, platform-independent window: the root of a UI tree. It owns its content (and an open modal), lays it out, routes pointer, key and text input, owns keyboard focus and the [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab) ring, shows popups and tooltips, and emits render commands, all without needing an OS window.

The app owns it, usually as a local in `main()`. ui::run(window) and [show()](#show) create the OS window for it from its [WindowOptions](window-options.md) and install its host, renderer and text measurer. Closing destroys the OS window and leaves the Window a valid object that can be shown again. Everything window-level the app configures (title, [WindowStyle](window-style.md), backdrop, icon, system menu, taskbar state) is stored here and applied once the OS window exists, so it can be set before or after [show()](#show). The first control that can take keyboard focus gets it when the window is activated. The window's actual state ([state()](#state), [active()](#active), [visible()](#visible), [caption_insets()](#caption_insets)) is written only by the host. The app asks for a change through [request_state()](#request_state) and similar functions and binds to the result.

Single-owner: [set_content()](#set_content) and [show_modal()](#show_modal) take a `std::unique_ptr` (or a `ui::` spec) and hand back a non-owning observer. Not copyable or movable. UI-thread only, except [post()](#post) and [ref()](#ref).

Example: 
```cpp
int main()
{
    ui::Window window{{.title = "Demo", .size = {480, 320}}};
    ui::Property<int> clicks{0};
    bool              unsaved = false;
    window.set_content(ui::VerticalStack{
        .spacing  = 12.0f,
        .content  = {
            ui::Text{.text = ui::bind(clicks, [](int n) { return std::format("Clicks: {}", n); })},
            ui::Button{.text = "Click me", .on_click = [&] { ++clicks; unsaved = true; }},
        },
    });
    window.on_closing([&] { return unsaved ? ui::Cancel : ui::Proceed; });
    return ui::run(window);
}
```

## Window

```cpp
Window(WindowOptions options = {})
```

A window with no content and no OS window yet, [Theme::light()](../themes/theme.md#light), [state()](#state) Normal. [`options`](#options) is what it will be created with; its title, style, backdrop, chrome, system menu and size limits become the Window's own properties right away.

## ~Window

```cpp
~Window()
```

Destroys the OS window too, if the window is still shown. Not from inside one of this window's own handlers: call [close()](#close) there instead.

## Window

```cpp
Window(const Window&) = delete
```

## operator=

```cpp
Window& operator=(const Window&) = delete
```

## set_content

```cpp
template <typename T>
T* set_content(std::unique_ptr<T> content, std::source_location where = std::source_location::current())
```

Take ownership of the content element and return a non-owning observer to it, valid until the content is replaced or the window destroyed. Replacing content drops focus, entered focus scopes, open popups and any open modal, since all of them pointed into the old tree, and bumps [content_generation()](#content_generation). The next [layout()](#layout) lays the new tree out. A null [`content`](#content) leaves the window empty.

Safe to call from a handler inside the content being replaced (a page's own "Next" button): the old tree is destroyed once the input or tick that ran the handler has returned.

`where` is for the thread check (ThreadCheck.hpp); leave it defaulted.

## set_content

```cpp
template <ui::SpecLike S>
Element* set_content(S&& spec, std::source_location where = std::source_location::current())
```

The declarative overload: hand [set_content()](#set_content) a spec (or a [ui::Spec](spec-vocabulary.md#class-spec) returned from a component function), e.g. `window.set_content(ui::VerticalStack{.spacing = 12, .content = {...}})`, and the window takes the tree it builds.

It returns Element*, since the spec's type is erased by the time it gets here. A spec's `.control` field gives a typed observer to any node inside the tree.

## content

```cpp
Element* content() const
```

The root of the content tree (non-owning), or nullptr before [set_content()](#set_content).

## show_modal

```cpp
template <typename T>
T* show_modal(std::unique_ptr<T> dialog, std::source_location where = std::source_location::current())
```

Show `dialog` modally over the content, taking ownership, and return a non-owning observer valid until [close_modal()](#close_modal) takes effect. [DialogControl](../controls/dialog.md#uidialogcontrol) is the usual one.

The modal is owned separately from the content and from popups opened with [Element::open_popup()](element.md#open_popup). An outside click doesn't dismiss it. While it is open, all pointer and key input goes to it and the [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab) ring covers only the modal. Focus goes to the dialog's [Element::default_focus()](element.md#default_focus) if that is in its ring, else its first stop, and is restored to whatever had it before once the modal closes (if that element is still in the tree). Showing a new modal replaces an open one, also from a handler of the open one; a null `dialog` closes the open one. `where` is for the thread check.

## show_modal

```cpp
template <ui::SpecLike S>
Element* show_modal(S&& spec, std::source_location where = std::source_location::current())
```

The declarative overload, mirroring [set_content()](#set_content)'s: builds `spec` (typically a [`ui::Dialog`](../controls/dialog.md#uidialog)) and shows the result modally. Use the spec's `.control` for a typed observer.

## close_modal

```cpp
void close_modal()
```

Close the open modal and restore the focus it interrupted. No-op if no modal is open. A [DialogControl](../controls/dialog.md#uidialogcontrol) closes itself, so this is for closing one from outside; its [on_closed()](#on_closed) then reports DialogResult::None. Safe to call from a callback inside the modal, such as a button's on_click. The modal is destroyed at the start of the next input dispatch or [layout()](#layout), after that callback has returned.

## has_modal

```cpp
bool has_modal() const
```

Whether a modal is open (a [close_modal()](#close_modal) still pending counts as open).

## modal

```cpp
Element* modal() const
```

The open modal (non-owning), or nullptr.

## content_generation

```cpp
std::uint64_t content_generation() const
```

A counter bumped by [set_content()](#set_content)/show_modal()/close_modal(), every point that can destroy part of the tree while the Window itself survives. Code that holds an Element* across calls, such as the accessibility provider, records the generation it saw and stops using the pointer once the counter has changed.

## visual_tree

```cpp
const VisualTree& visual_tree() const
```

The compact, data-oriented shape of the tree (stable VisualIds, dirty flags) as of the most recent [layout()](#layout) call; empty before the first one. Built when asked for, not by every layout pass.

## layout_pass_count

```cpp
std::size_t layout_pass_count() const
```

How many times [layout()](#layout) has run measure and arrange. A [layout()](#layout) call that finds nothing dirty skips the pass and doesn't count. Useful for checking that invalidation works.

## layout_size

```cpp
Size layout_size() const
```

The client size, in DIPs, passed to the most recent [layout()](#layout); zero before the first. [WindowOptions::size](window-options.md) is the size asked for at creation.

## theme

```cpp
const Theme& theme() const
```

The theme every control in the tree measures and draws with. [Theme::light()](../themes/theme.md#light) until the host reports the OS theme state, then the one resolved from [theme_request()](#theme_request), unless the app pinned one with [pin_theme()](#pin_theme).

## pin_theme

```cpp
void pin_theme(Theme theme)
```

Pins [`theme`](#theme): the window keeps it through OS theme changes (dark mode, accent color, contrast themes) until [set_theme()](#set_theme) hands the choice back. Bumps [theme_revision()](#theme_revision), so the host re-applies the frame colors and dark-mode caption. Takes effect on the next [layout()](#layout)/render(). A theme with [Theme::animations_enabled](../themes/theme.md#animations_enabled) off has its animation durations zeroed here, as [resolve_theme()](../themes/namespace-ui.md#resolve_theme) does.

## theme_request

```cpp
const ThemeRequest& theme_request() const
```

What the theme is resolved from; [WindowOptions::theme](window-options.md) until changed. The window re-resolves it whenever the OS theme state changes, unless [pin_theme()](#pin_theme) pinned a theme.

## set_theme

```cpp
void set_theme(ThemeRequest request)
```

Resolves the theme from `request` against the OS theme state last reported, and keeps following it. Unpins a theme set with [pin_theme()](#pin_theme).

## theme_pinned

```cpp
bool theme_pinned() const
```

Whether [pin_theme()](#pin_theme) pinned the current theme.

## theme_revision

```cpp
unsigned theme_revision() const
```

Bumped by every [pin_theme()](#pin_theme). The host checks it to notice a theme change the app made, such as a dark mode toggle, and then updates what the OS draws for the window: the caption colors from [Theme::chrome](../themes/theme.md#chrome) and the light or dark system backdrop.

## state

```cpp
const Property<WindowState>& state() const
```

The state the window is in, never the one last asked for. Only the host writes it (report_state()), so it is const here; bind to it as usual:

```cpp
ui::Button{
    .text = ui::bind(window.state(), [](ui::WindowState s) {
        return std::string{s == ui::WindowState::Fullscreen ? "Exit full screen" : "Full screen"}; }),
    .on_click = [w = &window] { w->toggle_fullscreen(); },
}
```

## restores_to

```cpp
const Property<WindowState>& restores_to() const
```

The state [restore()](#restore) would land in now: what Minimized or Fullscreen goes back to (Maximized, Normal, or Fullscreen for a window minimized from full screen), Normal from Maximized and from Normal. Written by the host with [state()](#state); bind to it for a caption button:

```cpp
ui::Button{
    .text = ui::bind(window.restores_to(), [](ui::WindowState s) {
        return std::string{s == ui::WindowState::Maximized ? "Restore to maximized" : "Restore"}; }),
    .on_click = [w = &window] { w->restore(); },
}
```

## request_state

```cpp
void request_state(WindowState state)
```

Ask the host for a state. The answer arrives later through [state()](#state), and may be a refusal. Without an OS window it becomes [options()](#options).initial_state, what the next one is shown in.

## restore

```cpp
void restore()
```

Back to what was there before Minimized or Fullscreen, or Maximized to Normal. Without an OS window, [options()](#options).initial_state goes back to Normal.

## toggle_fullscreen

```cpp
void toggle_fullscreen()
```

Fullscreen, or back out of it to the state it was entered from (the F11 idiom).

## close

```cpp
void close()
```

Close the window as its close button would, so [on_closing()](#on_closing) can still veto it. The one way out of a `Frame::None` window. No-op without a host.

## force_close

```cpp
void force_close()
```

Close the window without asking [on_closing()](#on_closing), otherwise as [close()](#close). The way to finish a close that [on_closing()](#on_closing) held back until the user confirmed it:

```cpp
bool unsaved = false; // set by the app's edits
window.on_closing([&] {
    if (!unsaved)
        return ui::Proceed;
    window.show_modal(ui::Dialog{
        .title     = "Save changes?",
        .primary   = {.text = "Save"},
        .secondary = {.text = "Don't save"},
        .close     = {.text = "Cancel"},
        .on_closed = [&](ui::DialogResult result) {
            if (result == ui::DialogResult::Primary)
                save();
            if (result != ui::DialogResult::Close)
                window.force_close();
        },
    });
    return ui::Cancel;
});
```

## on_closing

```cpp
void on_closing(Callback<Decision(const WindowClosingArgs&)> handler)
```

Asked before the window closes, however that was requested (close button, Alt+F4, the taskbar, [close()](#close)); return [ui::Cancel](../core/namespace-ui.md#cancel) to keep it open. One slot; empty, or a handler that returns nothing, lets the close through.

## on_closed

```cpp
void on_closed(Callback<void()> handler)
```

Called once as the window goes away, while this Window and its tree still exist. It's the place to stop and join worker threads that [post()](#post) to it: [post()](#post) drops its work from here on, until the window is shown again. The Window object itself stays valid after it closed; it is the app's to destroy.

## on_theme_changed

```cpp
void on_theme_changed(Callback<void(const Theme&)> handler)
```

Called after the theme was resolved again: the OS switched dark mode, accent color or contrast, or [set_theme()](#set_theme) or [pin_theme()](#pin_theme) asked for another. [theme()](#theme) is the new one, which may equal the old. For colors an app works out itself, such as a syntax highlighter's palette.

## end_menu_access

```cpp
bool end_menu_access()
```

Gives keyboard focus back to where it was before Alt, F10 or an Alt+letter moved it to a menu bar ([Element::take_menu_access()](element.md#take_menu_access)). A menu bar calls it on Escape and after running an item. False, and nothing changes, when focus didn't get there that way.

## placement

```cpp
std::optional<WindowPlacement> placement() const
```

The placement to persist ([WindowPlacement](window-placement.md)): where the window is, or where it was when it closed. Nullopt before the window was first shown. Read it after [`ui::run()`](namespace-ui.md#run) returns and hand it back through [`ui::WindowOptions::placement`](window-options.md) on the next run.

## move

```cpp
void move(Point position)
```

Move the outer top-left. Without an OS window it becomes [options()](#options).position, where the next one is created. A non-finite position is ignored.

## resize

```cpp
void resize(Size size)
```

Resize the client area, the room the content gets; the frame comes on top. A maximized, minimized or full-screen window stays as it is and takes the size when restored. Without an OS window it becomes [options()](#options).size, what the next one is created with. A negative, infinite or NaN size is ignored.

```cpp
std::optional<Rect> bounds() const
```

The window's position and size, as one rect; nullopt without a host.

## work_area

```cpp
std::optional<Rect> work_area() const
```

The work area of the display the window is mostly on; nullopt without a host.

## show

```cpp
void show()
```

Shows a hidden window and brings it to the front with focus. [visible()](#visible) follows once the host reports it.

## show_inactive

```cpp
void show_inactive()
```

Shows a hidden window without activating it: it stays behind the active window, and focus stays where it is.

## options

```cpp
WindowOptions& options()
```

What the OS window is created with. [`title`](#title), [`style`](#style), [`backdrop`](#backdrop), [`chrome`](#chrome), [`system_menu`](#system_menu), [`min_size`](#min_size) and [`max_size`](#max_size) were read by the constructor, so writing them here does nothing: change those with [set_title()](#set_title), [set_style()](#set_style), [set_backdrop()](#set_backdrop), [set_chrome()](#set_chrome), [set_system_menu()](#set_system_menu) and [set_size_limits()](#set_size_limits). The other fields are read when the OS window is created, so they are writable until then; a change after the window was shown only takes effect the next time it is created.

## options

```cpp
const WindowOptions& options() const
```

The same, read-only.

The operating system's handle of this window (an `HWND` on Windows), or null while it has none: before [ui::run()](namespace-ui.md#run) or [show()](#show) created it, and after it closed. For the OS calls libwinui does not wrap.

## hide


Takes the window off the screen, the taskbar and Alt+Tab, and keeps it, its tree and its state for the next [show()](#show).

## visible

```cpp
const Property<bool>& visible() const
```

Whether the window is shown. Host-written, like [state()](#state); false until a host reports the window shown.

## is_open

```cpp
const Property<bool>& is_open() const
```

Whether the window is open: true from the moment [ui::run()](namespace-ui.md#run) or [show()](#show) created it until it closes, hidden or not. Host-written, like [visible()](#visible), so it can be bound, a menu item's check mark following whether a tool window is open.

```cpp
void activate()
```

Brings the window to the front, with focus.

The minimum and maximum client sizes the user can drag the window to. Zero on an axis leaves it unconstrained; not applied while full screen.

## active

```cpp
const Property<bool>& active() const
```

Whether this is the foreground window, which a [TitleBar](../controls/title-bar.md#uititlebar) dims itself by. Host-written; false until a host reports the window activated.

## external_drag

```cpp
const Property<bool>& external_drag() const
```

Whether a drag from another app (files from Explorer, text from a browser) is over this window: true from when it enters until it leaves or drops, whichever drop target inside it the pointer is over. For drop zones that show only while something is dragged in; what is dragged is [external_drag_data()](#external_drag_data).

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Border{
    .visible = ui::bind(window.external_drag()),
    .content = ui::Text{.text = "Drop PDF files here"},
};
```

## scale

```cpp
const Property<float>& scale() const
```

Device pixels per DIP on the monitor the window is on: 1 at 100 %, 1.5 at 150 %, 2 at 200 %. Host-written, and it changes when the window moves to a monitor with another scale; 1 until a host reports one. For an image decoded at the size it is shown at, in pixels.

Example: 
```cpp
const float pixels = 160.0f * window.scale().get(); // a 160 DIP thumbnail, sharp at any scale
```

## external_drag_data

```cpp
const DataPackage* external_drag_data() const
```

What the drag from another app over this window carries, while [external_drag()](#external_drag) is true; nullptr otherwise. Valid until the drag leaves or drops.

The caption space an extended title bar must leave alone ([CaptionInsets](caption-insets.md)). Host-written; all zero unless [WindowStyle::extend_content_into_title_bar](window-style.md) is on.

## hit_region_at

```cpp
HitRegion hit_region_at(Point client_dips) const
```

Classify a window-client point for a host that lets content stand in for the caption (a `Frame::Borderless`, `Frame::None` or `Frame::Themed` window, or content extended into the title bar): Caption where a press should drag the window, a caption button or the system menu over a frame the theme draws, Client everywhere else. Asks the content tree through [Element::hit_region()](element.md#hit_region); an open modal or popup is always Client.

## cursor_at

```cpp
CursorShape cursor_at(Point client_dips) const
```

The pointer cursor at a window-client point. Starting at the innermost element under the point (in the topmost open popup, the modal, or the tree) and walking up its parents, the first element that asks for a cursor decides, through set_cursor() and then its own [cursor_at()](#cursor_at). The arrow is the default. While the left button is held, the cursor found at the press stays, since the pressed element has the pointer captured. During a drag, the arrow shows over a target that accepts it and the no-entry sign elsewhere. The host asks whenever the OS needs a cursor and after each pointer event.


The icon set with [set_icon()](#set_icon) or seeded from [`ui::WindowOptions::icon`](window-options.md), or nullopt, which shows the executable's first icon resource (or the system's default without one).

## set_icon

```cpp
void set_icon(std::optional<WindowIcon> icon)
```

## system_menu

```cpp
const std::vector<MenuItem>& system_menu() const
```

The app's own system-menu entries, in the order set. A toggle's or radio item's is_checked() is its current state.

## set_system_menu

```cpp
void set_system_menu(std::vector<MenuItem> items)
```

Replaces the app's system-menu entries. Call again to change a check mark.

The entries are the same [ui::MenuItem](../controls/menu-flyout.md#struct-menuitem) a menu takes, at the top level only: the OS menu shows the text, the check mark of a toggle or radio item, the disabled state and the separators, and drops icons, shortcuts and submenus. A pick invokes the item as a menu click would (a toggle flips, a radio item checks), and a bound field updates the entry live.

```cpp

```

Flash the taskbar button until the window is brought to the front or [cancel_attention()](#cancel_attention) is called. On a window already in front that is at once, so there is nothing to see; ask when [active()](#active) is false, e.g. when work finishes in the background.

## set_thumbnail_buttons

```cpp
void set_thumbnail_buttons(std::vector<ThumbnailButton> buttons)
```

Up to seven buttons under the taskbar thumbnail. The OS fixes the set on first use; a bound field, or a command's state, updates its button live, and a call with the same number of buttons replaces them ([ThumbnailButton](thumbnail-button.md)).

## layout

```cpp
void layout(Size client, const TextMeasurer& measurer)
```

Measures and arranges the content across a `client` sized area (or centered at its desired size, see [set_stretch_content()](#set_stretch_content)), then refreshes the focus ring, since the set of controls may have changed.

Does nothing while [state()](#state) is Minimized. A minimized window has a 0x0 client area, and laying out at that size would only collapse the tree until it is restored.

## set_parallel_layout

```cpp
void set_parallel_layout(ParallelLayout options)
```

Let [layout()](#layout) measure large batches of independent siblings on worker threads (see [ParallelLayout](parallel-layout.md)). On by default; `{.enabled = false}` keeps every measure on the UI thread. The layout is the same, bit for bit, either way.

## parallel_layout

```cpp
const ParallelLayout& parallel_layout() const
```

The parallel layout options [set_parallel_layout()](#set_parallel_layout) last set.

## set_stretch_content

```cpp
void set_stretch_content(bool stretch)
```

Arrange the content at the whole client size, where its own alignment and max size place it. On by default. Off centers the content at its desired size instead.

## stretch_content

```cpp
bool stretch_content() const
```

Whether the content is arranged at the whole client size (see [set_stretch_content()](#set_stretch_content)).

## set_background

```cpp
void set_background(std::optional<Color> background)
```

What the host fills the client area with before drawing the content, over the theme's `colors.background`; nullopt goes back to that. Not drawn while a system backdrop is on, which the host leaves transparent. A tray flyout uses it for the shell's flyout surface.

## background

```cpp
Color background() const
```

The effective client background: [set_background()](#set_background)'s color, else the theme's `colors.background`.

## render

```cpp
void render(Renderer& renderer) const
```

Emit render commands for the whole window, bottom to top: the content tree, connected animations, the popup layer (tooltips included), then an open modal. Does not paint [background()](#background); the host fills the client area first. Call after [layout()](#layout).

## render

```cpp
void render(Renderer& renderer, const Rect& clip) const
```

[render()](#render) for a frame that only repaints `clip` (window-client DIPs), one of the rects [take_damage()](#take_damage) returned: an element that drew nowhere near it last frame, and has not changed since, is skipped. Clipped to `clip` through the renderer; the host fills `clip` first.

## take_damage

```cpp
std::vector<Rect> take_damage()
```

What has to be painted again since the last call: the areas, in window-client DIPs, where the next frame differs from the last one (another color, text or place, gone or new). Elements don't have to mark themselves for this. Empty when nothing visible changed, and the whole client area for the first frame and after a change of size or background. Call after [layout()](#layout), once per frame, right before rendering those areas with render(renderer, clip).

## connected_animation_service

```cpp
ConnectedAnimationService& connected_animation_service()
```

The window's connected animations (ui/ConnectedAnimation.hpp), drawn above the tree and below the popups.

## tick

```cpp
bool tick(Duration delta)
```

Advances elapsed time by `delta`, driving every control's tick_override(), such as a tooltip's hover delay. The host calls this from its timer, so the window itself never reads a real clock. Returns whether the tree became dirty, so the caller knows whether to repaint.

## wants_ticks

```cpp
bool wants_ticks() const
```

Whether the last [tick()](#tick) found the window busy with time: something changed in it, an element called request_tick(), work was posted, a drag or a connected animation runs, or an [on_tick()](#on_tick) handler is set. A host that has seen no busy tick for a while stops ticking, so an idle window doesn't keep waking the process. A pending [after()](#after) or [every()](#every) timer, a tip waiting out its delay and an [Element::request_tick_in()](element.md#request_tick_in) don't make it busy, and [next_wake()](#next_wake) says when to tick for them. Neither does a change made only by such a timed step (a caret blink, an image's next frame), as long as nothing else was marked dirty since the last tick.

## next_wake

```cpp
std::optional<Duration> next_wake() const
```

How long until the window has to tick again, in [tick()](#tick) time, or 0 when that is overdue. It's the earliest of a pending [after()](#after) or [every()](#every) timer, the delay of a tip set with [Element::set_tool_tip()](element.md#set_tool_tip), and a wait an element asked for with [Element::request_tick_in()](element.md#request_tick_in) in the last [tick()](#tick) or frame. Nullopt when none of them is pending. A host ticks the window once at that time and not while it waits.

## on_tick

```cpp
void on_tick(Callback<void(Duration)> handler)
```

The app's own per-frame hook, so polling something (a worker's progress, a file watcher) doesn't take a custom [Element](element.md) just to get a tick_override(). Called at the start of every [tick()](#tick), before the controls' own tick_override(), with the same `delta`. There is no fixed rate. The window ticks after every input or system event it handles and at least every 100 ms while idle. One slot, like [on_key_preview()](#on_key_preview); an empty handler removes it.

## after

```cpp
Subscription after(Duration delay, Callback<void()> fn)
```

Runs `fn` once on the UI thread, `delay` from now, on the window's clock ([tick()](#tick)). The returned [Subscription](../core/subscription.md) owns the timer, and the timer ends with it: destroying or reset()ting it cancels the call, so keep it for as long as the call should still happen. A [Subscription](../core/subscription.md) left unstored is destroyed at once and the call never runs; for a call that needs no canceling, use [post_after()](#post_after). It runs on the first tick at or after its time, which while the window is otherwise idle comes at least every 100 ms. Time keeps running while the window is hidden or minimized; a closed window does not tick.

Example: 
```cpp
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
ui::Property<bool> saved{false};
ui::Subscription   hide_saved;
ui::Button{.text = "Save", .on_click = [&] {
    saved      = true;
    hide_saved = window.after(2s, [&] { saved = false; }); // a second click starts over
}};
```

## post_after

```cpp
void post_after(Duration delay, Callback<void()> fn)
```

Runs `fn` once on the UI thread, `delay` from now, as [after()](#after) does, with nothing to keep: the call cannot be canceled. It is dropped without running when the window closes first, and on a window that is closed already. Called on the UI thread, like [after()](#after); a worker thread hands work over with [post()](#post).

Example: 
```cpp
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
const std::string         link = "https://example.com/notes/42";
ui::Property<std::string> status;
ui::Button{.text = "Copy", .on_click = [&] {
    ui::clipboard().set_text(link);
    status = "Copied";
    window.post_after(2s, [&] { status = ""; });
}};
```

## every

```cpp
Subscription every(Duration interval, Callback<void()> fn)
```

Runs `fn` on the UI thread every `interval`, first one `interval` from now, until the returned [Subscription](../core/subscription.md) is destroyed or reset(). A late tick runs it once, not once for every interval it missed, and the next run is an interval after that. An interval of zero runs it on every tick.

Example: 
```cpp
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
ui::Property<int> seconds{0};
ui::Subscription  clock = window.every(1s, [&] { ++seconds; });
```

## add_command

```cpp
Subscription add_command(const Command& command)
```

Makes `command`'s `.shortcut` fire while this window has focus, whether or not a button or menu item offers the command, until the returned [Subscription](../core/subscription.md) is destroyed or reset(). A key the focused control or a shortcut of an area around it takes never reaches it. The command runs only while it is enabled, with an empty parameter.

Example: 
```cpp
ui::Command open{.text = "Open", .shortcut = ui::Ctrl + ui::Key::O, .execute = [&] { open_file(); }};
ui::Subscription keep_open = window.add_command(open);
```

## post

```cpp
void post(Callback<void()> work)
```

Run `work` on the UI thread at the start of the next [tick()](#tick), ahead of the [on_tick()](#on_tick) hook. Unlike every other member, this one may be called from any thread. It is how a worker hands its result back without the app polling for it: 
```
std::thread([home = window.ref(), path] {
    auto image = decode(path);
    home.post([image = std::move(image)]() mutable { show(std::move(image)); });
}).detach();
```

The thread holds a [WindowRef](window-ref.md), so work it posts after the window is gone is dropped and never reaches a destroyed object.

The host is woken, so the work doesn't wait for the idle timer.

Work posted after the window closed, or still queued then, is dropped without running. Dropped work is destroyed outside the window's lock: by the posting thread when [post()](#post) refuses it, by the UI thread as the window closes when it was still queued, so its destructor may post again.

As a member, this needs the Window to exist: called on a destroyed one it is undefined behavior. A worker that can outlive the Window posts through [ref()](#ref) instead ([WindowRef::post()](window-ref.md#post)), which drops the work once the Window is gone, as [`co_await ui::on_ui_thread(window.ref())`](namespace-ui.md#on_ui_thread) does.

The UI thread is the one that constructed the Window; a build with thread checks (ThreadCheck.hpp) reports any other member called from another thread.

## ref

```cpp
WindowRef ref() const noexcept
```

A weak handle to this Window for a worker that may outlive it: its [WindowRef::post()](window-ref.md#post) is [post()](#post) while this Window exists and drops the work once it is destroyed, also when another Window was built at the same address since. Callable from any thread while the Window exists.

## on_key_preview

```cpp
void on_key_preview(Callback<Handling(const KeyEvent&)> handler)
```

A window-wide shortcut: `handler` sees every key before [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab) handling, focus scopes and the focused element do, and returns [ui::Handled](../core/namespace-ui.md#handled) to consume it. It watches keys pass by, so a handler that returns nothing lets every key go on. One slot, for the app, such as an F11 full-screen toggle:

```cpp
window.on_key_preview([w = &window](const ui::KeyEvent& e) {
    if (e.key != ui::Key::F11 || e.action != ui::KeyAction::Down) return ui::NotHandled;
    w->toggle_fullscreen();
    return ui::Handled;
});
```

## focus_content

```cpp
void focus_content()
```

Focus the first stop in the tab ring. The window does this on its own when it is first activated, so call it only to send focus back to the start later on.

## focus_next

```cpp
void focus_next()
```

Advance focus to the next stop in the ring (wraps), as [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab) does.

## focus_previous

```cpp
void focus_previous()
```

Retreat focus to the previous stop (wraps), as Shift+Tab does.

## blur

```cpp
void blur()
```

Clear focus: no element has it afterwards.

## focus

```cpp
bool focus(Element& element)
```

Move keyboard focus to `element`, or, when it takes no focus itself (a panel, a view's host), to the first stop of the tab ring inside it. False, and focus stays where it was, when neither is a stop in this window right now: hidden, disabled or in another window. The same as [Element::focus()](element.md#focus).

## push_focus

```cpp
bool push_focus(Element& element)
```

[focus()](#focus) that remembers what had focus, for a view that takes the keyboard while it is open (a page view over a list): [pop_focus()](#pop_focus) gives focus back. False, and nothing is remembered, when [focus()](#focus) could not move focus.

Example: 
```cpp
void show_page(ui::Element& page_view)
{
    window.push_focus(page_view); // opening the view
    // ...
    window.pop_focus();           // closing it: back to the thumbnail that had focus
}
```

## pop_focus

```cpp
bool pop_focus()
```

Give focus back to what had it at the last [push_focus()](#push_focus) that is not yet popped. False when nothing was pushed, or what had focus is gone or no longer a stop; focus then stays put.

## suspend_focus

```cpp
void suspend_focus()
```

The host window lost keyboard focus: clear focus, remembering which stop had it.

## restore_focus

```cpp
void restore_focus()
```

The host window got keyboard focus back: refocus the stop [suspend_focus()](#suspend_focus) remembered if it is still in the ring, otherwise the first stop, as [focus_content()](#focus_content) does.

## focused

```cpp
Element* focused() const
```

The element with keyboard focus (non-owning), or nullptr.

## caret_bounds

```cpp
std::optional<Rect> caret_bounds() const
```

Where text typed now would go: the focused element's [Element::caret_bounds()](element.md#caret_bounds), in client DIPs, or nullopt. The backend keeps an input method's candidate window and the emoji panel there.

## focus_element

```cpp
bool focus_element(Element* e)
```

Focuses `e` if it is in the tab-focus ring and returns true. Otherwise does nothing and returns false. Unlike [focus()](#focus), it doesn't look for a stop inside `e`. [Accessibility](accessibility.md) clients set focus through it.

## enter_focus_scope

```cpp
bool enter_focus_scope(Element* scope)
```

Step *into* `scope`, making its own inner ring the tab ring until the matching exit: [Tab](../controls/tabs.md#uitab) then cycles only within it and Escape steps back out onto `scope` itself. Refuses (returns false, changing nothing) unless `scope` is a focus scope sitting in the current ring with a non-empty inner ring of its own, which lets the key that would have entered fall through to the element's ordinary handle_key() instead. Scopes nest: entering one inside an entered scope pushes onto the stack.

## exit_focus_scope

```cpp
bool exit_focus_scope()
```

Step back out of the innermost entered scope, restoring focus to the scope element. Returns false when no scope is entered.

## entered_focus_scope

```cpp
Element* entered_focus_scope() const
```

The innermost entered scope, or nullptr when the tab ring is the whole tree.
